proxy_language: Proto-Malayo-Polynesian (with Proto-Austronesian lexical models); secondary substrate flavour from Proto-Central-Malayo-Polynesian / Proto-South-Halmahera-West-New-Guinea for Wallacea
proxy_rationale: Pleistocene-Holocene foragers of Sundaland and Wallacea (c. 50,000-4,000 BP) left no linguistic record. Their languages are lost; the later Austronesian expansion (c. 4,000-3,000 BP) replaced or absorbed them, and Papuan (Trans-New Guinea, West Papuan) languages survive in parts of Wallacea (Timor-Alor-Pantar, North Halmahera). Austronesian is the only well-reconstructed, regionally dominant language family for the area, so Proto-Malayo-Polynesian is used purely as a phonological and morphological model for plausible, pronounceable names. It is NOT a claim that the foragers spoke Austronesian. Negrito-associated forager languages (Aslian, Philippine Negrito) are also Austronesian/Austroasiatic later layers and add little extra.
phonology: Proto-Malayo-Polynesian consonants (Blust/ACD notation): *p *t *k *b *d *g *j *z *s *h *m *n *\u00f1 *\u014b *l *R *r *w *y *q (plus *C, *c variably). Vowels *a *i *u *e (schwa, written e). Diphthongs *ay *aw *uy *iw. Simplified for game use: p t k b d g s h m n ng ny l r w y plus a i u e o. Stress penultimate (PMP).
phonotactics: Dominant canonical shape: disyllabic roots (C)V(C)CV(C), i.e. CVCVC, CVCV, CVC.CVC. Syllable types V, CV, CVC. Root-final consonants allowed (typically p t k b d g s h m n ng l r, with *q, *R lost or reflexed in daughters). Medial clusters are only homorganic nasal+stop (mp nt nk mb nd ng-g) or a few liquids/sibilants (rk, lt, st), usually across syllable boundary. No word-initial clusters. No vowel-initial restrictions. Roots rarely exceed 3 syllables before affixation; reduplication common.
orthography: Practical Latin transliteration in the style of the Austronesian Comparative Dictionary: ng for velar nasal, ny for palatal nasal, e for schwa, q/h/R marked in reconstruction; for names use plain a e i o u, p t k b d g s h m n ng ny l r w y. No diacritics, no c/f/v/x/z/q in game names. Use hyphen only for affix boundaries or compound joins.
morphology: Roots mostly disyllabic nouns/verbs, lexical category fluid. Affixation: prefixes ma- (stative/adjectival), pa- (causative/instrument), ka- (abstract/collective), ta-, pi-/pa-; infix -um- (actor), -in- (patient/nominalizer); suffixes -an (place/locative nominalizer), -en/-i (applicative/patient). Reduplication: full (ikan-ikan 'many fish/small fish') or CV- partial (plural, diminutive, intensive). Personal-name marker *si, common-noun article *u / *i. No noun classes or case on nouns beyond preposed markers. Numerals/classifiers minimal.
compounding: Head-initial: modified noun comes first, modifier follows (Austronesian pattern): 'house of fire' = noun + noun. Genitive/attributive constructions juxtapose head + possessor (*balay *banua 'village house') or use *ni / *na linker for possessor. Agent/maker nouns use pa- or pa-...-an for 'place of', tu- or pan- for 'one who does'. Place names often use *banua 'land/community', *Rumaq 'house', *wahiR 'river', *bukit 'hill', *laut 'sea'. Adjectives follow nouns (ma- stative: *qitem 'black').
noun_phrase_order: Head noun first, then modifier(s): N + Adj, N + N(possessor), N + Dem. Numerals precede noun. Articles/markers precede head.
sources: Blust, Robert & Trussel, Stephen. Austronesian Comparative Dictionary (ACD), online, ongoing
Blust, Robert. The Austronesian Languages (revised edition), 2013
Adelaar, K. Alexander & Himmelmann, Nikolaus (eds.). The Austronesian Languages of Asia and Madagascar, 2005
Wurm, Stephen & Hattori, Shiro. Language Atlas of the Pacific Area, 1981
Glottolog and ASJP databases for Wallacea languages
Wiktionary Proto-Austronesian and Proto-Malayo-Polynesian reconstruction pages

notes: The actual Pleistocene-Holocene forager languages of Sundaland and Wallacea are unrecoverable; names built here are an Austronesian-flavoured stand-in and carry no claim of genetic or historical continuity. Wallacean Papuan influence (Timor-Alor-Pantar, Halmahera) could justify occasional final-vowel-free closed syllables, but is not modelled. No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word since the language is not Goidelic. Note: worked_examples above use Malay-style spellings (rumah, wair) as approximate reflexes of reconstructed forms; keep h instead of reconstructed *q/*R and use vowel-final or -k/-n/-ng/-r/-l/-s/-h/-m/-p/-t finals.
